# Isigili Sutta (MN 116 (PTS MN iii 68))

**ID:** MN 116 (PTS MN iii 68)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Isigili Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** At Isigili
**PTS:** MN iii 68
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Isigili Sutta* (MN 116; PTS MN iii 68) is set at Mount Isigili near Rājagaha [Ray 1994; Walker 2018]. Reflecting on the impermanence of geographical features, the Buddha relates how five hundred *paccekabuddhas* (solitary or silent buddhas) formerly dwelled on Mount Isigili [Jantrasrisalai 2008; Walker 2018]. In the discourse, these figures are presented as *ṛṣis* (*isi*) and contrasted with ordinary mortals (*manussa*) [Ray 1994]. Structurally, the text provides an enumeration of the names of these past sages in prose followed by an expanded metric list in verse, concluding with an exhortation to pay homage to them [Norman 1983; Walker 2018]. Modern philologists note that the third *paṇṇāsa* of the *Majjhimanikāya*, within which the sutta is preserved, includes material of relatively late composition, and Norman suggests that the systematized lists of *paccekabuddhas* in MN 116 reflect later developments or borrowings in early Buddhist literature [Norman 1983].

A direct parallel to the sutta is found in the Chinese *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 38.7) [Anālayo 2010].

Beyond canonical study, the *Isigili Sutta* occupies an important role in protective (*paritta*) ritual culture [Global Recovery 2010; Walker 2018]. In Sri Lanka, it is included in the Book of Protection (*Pirith Potha*) as one of five special *parittas* recited to heal and dispel illness [Global Recovery 2010]. In Southeast Asian manuscript traditions, such as Cambodian chanted accordion books (*leporellos*), the text is preserved for liturgical recitation and organized into three melodic recitation units (*pad*), dividing the opening prose and the subsequent poetic verses [Walker 2018].

**Sources**

- [Ray 1994] Reginald A. Ray, Buddhist Saints in India: A Study in Buddhist Values and Orientations (1994) — Discussed the sutta's hagiographical role concerning paccekabuddhas and the contrast between isi and manussa.
- [Norman 1983] K. R. Norman, Pāli Literature (1983) — Described the prose and verse structure and discussed the relative lateness of the text and the paccekabuddha concept.
- [Jantrasrisalai 2008] Chanida Jantrasrisalai, Early Buddhist Dhammakaya (2008) — Noted the story of five hundred paccekabuddhas dwelling at Mount Isigili.
- [Global Recovery 2010] Symposium, Global Recovery: The Buddhist Perspective (2010) — Documented the use of the Isigili Sutta in Sri Lankan pirith healing rituals.
- [Walker 2018] Trent Walker, Unfolding Buddhism: Communal Scripts, Localized Translations, and the Work of the Dying in Cambodian Chanted Leporellos (2018) — Detailing the sutta's summary, liturgical divisions (pad), and role in paritta collections and Cambodian leporellos.
- [Anālayo 2010] Bhikkhu Anālayo, 'Paccekabuddhas in the Isigili-sutta and its Ekottarika-āgama Parallel' (2010) — Referenced comparative studies between MN 116 and its Ekottarika-āgama counterpart.
